text: A quantum simulation that gives a different answer every time you run it isn't a simulation you can trust, publish, or debug. The fix isn't to avoid randomness, measurement sampling and noise models genuinely need it, it's to make the randomness itself reproducible.

A pseudo-random number generator is actually a fully deterministic algorithm that just produces output that looks statistically random. np dot random dot default underscore r n g of a seed is the modern, recommended way to get one in NumPy. This matters constantly in quantum code: reproducing a measurement-sampling histogram, reproducing a variational algorithm's random initial parameters, and reproducing exactly which noise occurred on which qubit. And the law of large numbers gives you a deterministic sanity check even though individual samples are genuinely random.

Seeding default underscore r n g with forty-two and drawing five random values, then seeding it again with the same forty-two and drawing five more, gives back np dot array_equal returning True — both runs, same seed, produce the identical sequence. A seed guarantees that the same seed on the same NumPy version reproduces the same numbers, nothing more and nothing less.

If a simulated coin has true probability point five of heads and you flip it ten thousand times, the expected count of heads is exactly ten thousand times point five, five thousand point zero. That's exact arithmetic, not a random draw, it's what the average of many random runs should converge toward. The right thing to test is that a sampled count lands close to five thousand within statistical noise, not that it hits exactly one specific number.

Next lesson moves from reproducible randomness to reproducible structure: organizing a scientific computing project so a notebook's exploratory code doesn't quietly become the only copy of a result nobody can rerun.
